The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $n\ge1$
and let $e_k(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,k\cdot x)$, $k\in\mathbb Z^n$, be the coordinate
characters on $\mathbb T^n$
([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]],
[[def-fourier-coefficients-and-trigonometric-polynomials]]). Then:

1. $(e_k)_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}$ is an orthonormal family in the complex Hilbert
   space $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
2. it is an orthonormal basis: its closed linear span is $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$;
3. consequently the Fourier expansion
   $f=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)e_k$ and Parseval's identity
   $$\|f\|_2^2=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}|\widehat f(k)|^2,\qquad \langle f,g\rangle=\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^n}\widehat f(k)\overline{\widehat g(k)}$$
   hold for all $f,g\in L^2(\mathbb T^n)$, in the finite-subset-net sense; and
4. the Fourier coefficient map is a surjective linear isometry of
   $L^2(\mathbb T^n)$ onto $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^n,\mathbb C)$.

No Hilbert tensor-product identification is used anywhere.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
The space $L^p(\mu)$ as the quotient by null functions and
Complex Lp classes and Euclidean test-function conventions. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
The $L^p$ norm descends to the quotient and makes $L^p$ a normed space for $1 \le p \le \infty$
for real scalars and
Complex Holder, Minkowski, and the quotient norm for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
Weak derivative of a locally integrable function. Under
The Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$), local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
Weak differentiation ignores null-set changes, while
Uniqueness of a weak derivative as an almost-everywhere class gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

For a smooth real function $f$, its **Riemannian gradient** is $\operatorname{grad}_g f=(df)^\sharp$.

[[prop-exterior-derivative-of-a-function-is-its-differential]] identifies $df(X)=Xf$. The smooth bundle isomorphism in [[thm-the-musical-maps-are-smooth-inverse-bundle-isomorphisms]] therefore makes the gradient a smooth vector field. In coordinates $(\operatorname{grad}_g f)^i=\sum_jg^{ij}\partial_jf$. Constants, and all functions in dimension zero, have zero gradient.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. At each interior point, the
**Laplace–Beltrami operator** of $g$ is defined by the metric trace of the Hessian,
$$\Delta_gf(p):=\operatorname{tr}_g(\operatorname{Hess}f)_p:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i),$$
where $n=\dim M$ and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is any $g_p$-orthonormal basis of $T_pM$; the
trace of a bilinear form with respect to a positive-definite inner product does not
depend on that choice, so $\Delta_gf$ is well-defined and smooth in the interior;
when $f$ is smooth up to the boundary, it has the usual one-sided extension there.
Here
$\operatorname{Hess}f(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\operatorname{grad}f,Y)$ is the Levi-Civita
Hessian of
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]].

Equivalently, and with the **positive-divergence convention** of this library,
$$\Delta_gf=\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f),$$
where $\operatorname{div}_gX=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_vX)$ is the Riemannian
divergence of [[def-riemannian-divergence]] as computed in
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]]. The equivalence is the
pointwise computation
$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$
the middle sum being the endomorphism trace of $v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f$
in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with
$\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f)$; no local coordinates are needed and no
analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold
both sides are the empty sum $0$, and on a manifold with boundary the operator is defined
at interior points, with the usual one-sided extension at boundary points when $f$ is
smooth up to the boundary.

**This definition is the pointwise geometric operator only.** It records the trace
formula, the divergence form and the sign convention
$\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\circ\operatorname{grad}$ fixed by
[[def-riemannian-divergence]]. It does not assert any analytic conclusion about
harmonic functions on manifolds — no maximum principle, no Harnack inequality, no
boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed
on a general Riemannian manifold merely by writing down this definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice for the Sobolev interfaces used by consumers of this
definition. Let $k\ge1$ and $n\ge2$. A **bounded $C^k$ domain** in
$\mathbb R^n$ is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ with
the following local graph property. For every boundary point
$x\in\partial\Omega$ there are an open neighbourhood
$W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ of $x$, a rigid motion $R(p)=Qp+b$ with orthogonal
$Q$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, an open ball $B\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-1}$, and a
function $h\in C^k(B;\mathbb R)$ such that, after shrinking $W$ so that
$R(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R$,
$$R(\Omega\cap W)=R(W)\cap\{(y,s)\in B\times\mathbb R:s<h(y)\}.$$
In the coordinates $z=R(p)$ the domain therefore lies locally strictly below
the graph $s=h(y)$, and the boundary is that graph. The graph convention,
including the requirement that the domain occupy exactly the one-sided
subgraph, is the one of
[[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]; the
regularity $h\in C^k$ is the only strengthening here, and connectedness is not
required.

Write $R(p)=(y,s)$. The **flattening chart** is
$$\Phi:W\longrightarrow\Phi(W)\subseteq B\times\mathbb R,\qquad \Phi(p)=(y,s-h(y)),$$
with inverse $\Phi^{-1}(y,t)=R^{-1}(y,t+h(y))$ on $\Phi(W)$. Thus
$\Phi(\Omega\cap W)=\Phi(W)\cap\{t<0\}$. Both maps are of class $C^k$; the
coordinate shear $(y,s)\mapsto(y,s-h(y))$ has Jacobian determinant one. If
$B'\subset\overline{B'}\subset B$ is a compactly contained concentric ball,
then every derivative $D^\beta h$ with $|\beta|\le k$ is continuous on
$\overline{B'}$, hence bounded there, and consequently the derivatives
through order $k$ of $\Phi$ and of $\Phi^{-1}$ are bounded on the corresponding
compact patch. This is the precise sense in which a boundary chart is said to
have bounded derivatives through order $k$ on the compact patches used; it
does not assert any bound uniform in the chart, the point, or a boundary
atlas.

In dimension $n=1$, the bounded sets satisfying this local one-sided condition
are finite disjoint unions of bounded open intervals. Each endpoint has an
interval neighbourhood on which the domain occupies one side; the coordinate
is the identity or its reflection, and the graph function and derivative
bounds are vacuous. General bounded open subsets of $\mathbb R$ need not have
this property. A bounded $C^1$ domain in the
sense of [[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]] is a
bounded $C^1$ domain in this sense when $n\ge2$.

This definition asserts no extension theorem, no trace operator, and no
uniformity of chart constants: it fixes only the regularity of the boundary
and the exact one-sided graph convention that later local statements use.

derivations.claim: Choose boundary normal coordinates $(y,x_n)$ near $x_0$, with $x_n=\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)$ and inward unit normal $\partial_{x_n}$. The induced metric on the boundary is smooth. Choose a smooth hypersurface $S$ in $\partial\Omega$ through $x_0$, orthogonal there to $\xi_0$ (if $n=2$, take $S=\{x_0\}$). The boundary geodesics starting normally from $S$ give, by smooth dependence of the geodesic ODE and the inverse function theorem, coordinates $(s,z)$ near $x_0$; define $\phi(s,z)=s$. Gauss' lemma gives $|d\phi|_{g_{\partial\Omega}}=1$ and $d\phi(x_0)=\xi_0$. Shrink the patch so these coordinates and $\chi$ are supported inside it.

In boundary normal coordinates, $g^{nn}=1$ and $g^{n\alpha}=0$ at the boundary. Set $\Phi|_{x_n=0}=\phi$ and $\partial_n\Phi|_{x_n=0}=i$. Then $g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi=0$ at $x_n=0$ because $|d\phi|=1$. Differentiate this eikonal equation successively in $x_n$. At each order the newest unknown normal jet $\partial_n^{j+1}\Phi|_{x_n=0}$ occurs linearly with coefficient $2i g^{nn}=2i\ne0$; all other terms use already assigned jets and derivatives of $g$. Solve recursively for every normal jet. Realize the resulting jet sequence by the following local Borel construction: if $c_j(y)$ is the prescribed $j$th normal derivative, choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\theta$ equal to one near zero and supported in $(-1,1)$, and set $$\Phi(y,x_n)=\sum_{j\geq0}\frac{c_j(y)}{j!}x_n^j\theta(x_n/\varepsilon_j).$$ For all sufficiently large $j$, choose $\varepsilon_j<2^{-j}$ so that every derivative of order at most $j/2$ of the $j$th summand has sup norm at most $2^{-j}$; this is possible because those derivatives are bounded by constants times $\varepsilon_j^{j-m}$ with $m\leq j/2$. Choose any positive $\varepsilon_j$ for the finitely many smaller $j$. For each fixed derivative order, the tail then converges uniformly, so $\Phi$ is smooth and has the prescribed jets. In particular, the eikonal expression vanishes to infinite order at the boundary. Since $\partial_n\operatorname{Im}\Phi=1$ there, shrinking the collar gives $\operatorname{Im}\Phi\geq x_n/2$.

For $P_\gamma=\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla)$, direct differentiation gives $$P_\gamma(e^{i\lambda\Phi}b)=e^{i\lambda\Phi}\big[-\lambda^2p_\gamma b+i\lambda L_\gamma b+P_\gamma b\big],$$ where $p_\gamma=\gamma g^{ij}\partial_i\Phi\partial_j\Phi$ and $L_\gamma b=2\gamma g^{ij}(\partial_i\Phi)(\partial_jb)+\operatorname{div}(\gamma\nabla\Phi)b$. The phase is common to both conductivities and $p_\gamma=\gamma p_1$ vanishes to infinite order on the boundary by step 2.1. Prescribe $b_{0,\gamma}|_{\partial\Omega}=\chi$ and $b_{-j,\gamma}|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ for $j\geq1$. In boundary normal coordinates the coefficient of the new normal derivative in $L_\gamma b$ is $2i\gamma$, which is nonzero. Therefore the normal derivatives of $b_{0,\gamma}$ can be chosen successively so that $L_\gamma b_{0,\gamma}=0$ to infinite order at the boundary; after choosing $b_{0,\gamma},\ldots,b_{-(j-1),\gamma}$, the same recursion chooses all jets of $b_{-j,\gamma}$ so that $iL_\gamma b_{-j,\gamma}+P_\gamma b_{-(j-1),\gamma}=0$ to infinite order. Realize each sequence by the Borel series in step 2.1 and multiply by a fixed collar cutoff equal to one near the boundary support. Repeat for $\widetilde\gamma$.

Let $b_{\lambda,\gamma}=\sum_{j=0}^K\lambda^{-j}b_{-j,\gamma}$, with the same construction for $\widetilde\gamma$. The order-$\lambda^2$ eikonal term and the order-$\lambda,\ldots,\lambda^{1-K}$ transport terms in step 3.1 vanish to infinite order at $x_n=0$. Thus each remaining coefficient is $O(x_n^R)$ for every prescribed integer $R$. On the collar, $|e^{i\lambda\Phi}|\leq e^{-\lambda x_n/2}$. For every fixed $a,R$, direct integration gives $$\|\lambda^a x_n^R e^{-\lambda x_n/2}\|_{L^2(0,\delta)}=O(\lambda^{a-R-1/2}).$$ Choose $R$ and then $K$ large enough to make every residual term $O(\lambda^{-N})$. Derivatives of the collar cutoff are supported where $x_n\geq c>0$ and hence contribute $O(e^{-c\lambda})$. The same Gaussian integration shows $\|v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_{L^2}=O(\lambda^{-1})$ and bounds its gradient norm above. Thus the $H^1$ norms are bounded above and the residual bounds hold for the arbitrary prescribed $N$.

Let $r_\lambda=u_{\lambda,\gamma}-v_{\lambda,\gamma}\in H_0^1(\Omega)$. Its weak equation is $P_\gamma r_\lambda=-P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}$. Test with $r_\lambda$, use $\gamma\geq\gamma_*>0$, and use the Poincare inequality in [F3]: $$\gamma_*\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2^2\leq\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|r_\lambda\|_2 \leq C_P\|P_\gamma v_{\lambda,\gamma}\|_2\|\nabla r_\lambda\|_2.$$ If the last gradient norm is zero then $r_\lambda=0$ by [F3]; otherwise divide by it. This proves $\|r_\lambda\|_{H^1}=O(\lambda^{-N})$. The same argument applies to $\widetilde\gamma$.

In the collar, write $J(y,x_n)dS(y)dx_n$ for Euclidean volume in boundary normal coordinates, with $J(y,0)=1$. Since $\Phi=\phi+ix_n+O(x_n^2)$, $\operatorname{Im}\Phi=x_n+O(x_n^2)$ and $g(d\Phi,\overline{d\Phi})=2+O(x_n)$. The boundary values of both leading amplitudes are $\chi$, and lower amplitudes vanish there. Differentiating $v_{\lambda,\gamma}$ and $v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}$ therefore gives $$\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}\cdot\overline{\nabla v_{\lambda,\widetilde\gamma}} =2\lambda e^{-2\lambda x_n}|\chi(y)|^2+e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(1)+ e^{-2\lambda x_n}O(\lambda x_n),$$ uniformly for $0\leq x_n\leq\lambda^{-1/2}$. On this shrinking collar $\lambda x_n^2\leq1$, so after $t=\lambda x_n$ the phase remainder factor is uniformly bounded; boundedness of $F,J,\chi$ gives an integrable majorant $C t^ke^{-t}$ for the rescaled leading term. For each fixed $t$, the rescaled leading term tends to $2t^ke^{-2t}F(y,0)|\chi(y)|^2$. Each displayed remainder has an additional factor $\lambda^{-1}$ after scaling and is dominated by $C\lambda^{-1}(t^k+t^{k+1}+t^{k+2})e^{-t}$, including the phase error $e^{O(t^2/\lambda)}-1=O(t^2/\lambda)$; its integral tends to zero. On the rest of the fixed collar, $\operatorname{Im}\Phi\geq x_n/2$ gives exponential decay $e^{-\lambda x_n}\leq e^{-\sqrt{\lambda}}$; every polynomial prefactor is therefore negligible. The cutoff region away from the collar is also exponentially small. Thus the limit for approximate beams is $$2\int_0^\infty t^ke^{-2t}\,dt\int_{\partial\Omega}F|\chi|^2\,dS,$$ whose constant is strictly positive.

Taking equal conductivities, $F=1$, and $k=0$ in step 5.2 gives $\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\int_\Omega|\nabla v_{\lambda,\gamma}|^2dx=c_0\int_{\partial\Omega}|\chi|^2dS>0$. Together with the upper bound in step 4.1 this proves the asserted two-sided $H^1$ norm bound.

The exact corrections satisfy $H^1$ errors $O(\lambda^{-N})$ by step 5.1, while both approximate beams have uniformly bounded $H^1$ norms by step 4.1. Cauchy-Schwarz bounds the change in the weighted product integral, after multiplication by $\lambda^k$, by $C\lambda^k\lambda^{-N}$ because $0\leq\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Omega)^k\leq C$ on the bounded domain. Choose $N>k$. The error tends to zero, so the same limit holds for the exact solutions.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. For an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. For real scalars, define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous linear dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$. For complex scalars, define it as the continuous conjugate-linear dual: its pairing with $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ is linear in the dual element and conjugate-linear in $h$, using the Riemannian boundary density. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded open set and let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ is
compactly embedded in $L^p(\Omega)$: the inclusion is bounded, and every
sequence bounded in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging in
$L^p(\Omega)$. No regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is needed.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of
[[def-bounded-c-k-domain-and-boundary-charts]], let $\partial\Omega$ carry the
chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and
[[lem-surface-integral-is-independent-of-c-one-boundary-charts]], let
$1\le p<\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then there is a
unique bounded linear operator
$$T:W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow L^p(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $Tu=u|_{\partial\Omega}$ for every
$u\in C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and it satisfies
$\|Tu\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$. On each
boundary chart the operator is the flat half-space trace of
[[thm-trace-estimate-on-the-half-space]] transported by the flattening
diffeomorphism, and the chartwise definitions agree on overlaps; uniqueness
holds because two bounded operators agreeing on the dense subspace
$C(\overline\Omega)\cap W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ are equal.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$, $\theta=1-1/p$, and let $T$ be the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]]. Then there is
a bounded linear operator
$$R:W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega;\mathbb K)\longrightarrow W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$$
with $T\circ R=\mathrm{id}_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$ and
$\|Rg\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
Moreover, for every open neighbourhood $U$ of $\partial\Omega$ in
$\mathbb R^n$ there is such an operator $R_U$ whose image is contained in the
classes vanishing a.e. outside $U$, with
$\|R_Ug\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p,U)\|g\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}$.
The right inverse is not unique and no canonical choice is claimed.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ be a bounded
$C^{k+2}$ domain, $n\ge2$, $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let
$k\ge0$, let $L,a$ be as in
[[def-uniformly-elliptic-divergence-form-operator]] with
$a^{ij}\in W^{k+1,\infty}(\Omega)$, $b^i,c\in W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ and all
coefficient derivatives bounded, and let $f\in H^k(\Omega)$. If
$u\in H^1_0(\Omega)$ is a weak solution of $Lu=f$ with zero boundary values
([[def-weak-dirichlet-solution-for-a-divergence-form-operator]]), then
$u\in H^{k+2}(\Omega)$ and
$$\|u\|_{H^{k+2}(\Omega)}\le C\big(\|f\|_{H^k(\Omega)}+\|u\|_{L^2(\Omega)}\big),$$
with $C$ depending only on $n,k,\Omega$ and the coefficient bounds. The
derivative gain is exactly two orders; the boundary regularity required at
order $k$ is $C^{k+2}$, the coefficient regularity one order above the data
order, and the companion page records the sharp two-derivative example. For
$k=0$ the theorem is
[[thm-global-h-two-dirichlet-regularity]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega$ be a bounded $W^{k,p}$-extension domain, $k\ge1$ and $1\le p<\infty$. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Then:

1. if $kp<n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every $q$ with $\frac1q\ge\frac1p-\frac kn$ (equivalently $1\le q\le\frac{np}{n-kp}$);
2. if $kp=n$, $\|u\|_{L^q(\Omega)}\le C(q)\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$ for every finite $q$;
3. if $kp>n$, then for every integer $m\ge0$ and every $0<\alpha<1$ with $m+\alpha<k-\frac np$ there is a representative in $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ with $\|u\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}\le C\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}$; when $k-\frac np\notin\mathbb Z$ one may take $m=\lfloor k-\frac np\rfloor$ and $\alpha=k-\frac np-m$.

Here $C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)$ uses the continuous derivatives of the constructed representative on an ambient neighbourhood of $\overline\Omega$, with norm
$$\|g\|_{C^{m,\alpha}(\overline\Omega)}:=\sum_{|\beta|\le m}\sup_{\overline\Omega}|D^\beta g|+\sum_{|\beta|=m}\sup_{\substack{x,y\in\overline\Omega\\x\ne y}}\frac{|D^\beta g(x)-D^\beta g(y)|}{|x-y|^\alpha}.$$
For $\Omega=\varnothing$ set these norm values to $0$. The proof supplies such an ambient representative, so no boundary differentiability or regularity of $\partial\Omega$ is assumed.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1<p<\infty$ and $\theta=1-1/p$, with
$W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$ as in
[[def-fractional-sobolev-space-on-a-compact-c-one-boundary]]. Then the trace
operator $T$ of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] satisfies
$$\|Tu\|_{W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)}\le C(\Omega,p)\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)} \qquad(u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)),$$
and it is onto: $T(W^{1,p}(\Omega))=W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$. For $p>1$
the range is a strict subset of $L^p(\partial\Omega)$, and the trace is not a
compact operator into $W^{\theta,p}(\partial\Omega)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain and $1\le p<\infty$. Then the kernel of the trace
operator of [[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]] equals the
zero-boundary Sobolev space:
$$\{u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):Tu=0\}=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),$$
the $W^{1,p}$-closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$
([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$, be a
bounded $C^1$ domain, $1\le p<\infty$, and let $T$ be the trace operator of
[[thm-lp-trace-operator-on-a-bounded-c-one-domain]].

(i) If $\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$, then
$T(\eta u)=(\eta|_{\partial\Omega})\,Tu$ in $L^p(\partial\Omega)$ for every
$u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, and
$\|T(\eta u)\|_{L^p(\partial\Omega)}\le C_\eta\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$.

(ii) If $\Omega'\subseteq\Omega$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain and
$\partial\Omega\cap\partial\Omega'$ is relatively open in $\partial\Omega$,
then $(Tu)|_{\partial\Omega\cap\partial\Omega'}=T_{\Omega'}(u|_{\Omega'})$
a.e. for every $u\in W^{1,p}(\Omega)$, where $T_{\Omega'}$ is the trace
operator relative to $\Omega'$; in particular the trace is local and
compatible with restrictions to subdomains.

(iii) If a boundary chart $\Phi$ flattens a neighbourhood of a boundary point,
then for $u$ supported in a compact ambient patch inside that chart the transported trace
equals $T_+$ of the zero-extended flattened function after reflecting $t\mapsto-t$ and the corresponding boundary $L^p$ norms
agree up to the chart Jacobian.

There is a constant $C_P$ such that $\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq C_P\|
abla w\|_{L^2(M)}$ for $w\in H_0^1(M)$. Otherwise choose $w_j\in H_0^1(M)$ with $\|w_j\|_{L^2}=1$ and $\|
abla w_j\|_{L^2}	o0$. A finite chart partition and [F2] give an $L^2$-convergent subsequence. On compact $M$, the fixed finite chartwise $H^1$ norm is equivalent to $\|\cdot\|_{L^2}+\|
abla_g\cdot\|_{L^2}$ by bounded metric coefficients, so this subsequence is Cauchy in $H^1$ and converges to some $w\in H_0^1(M)$ with $\|w\|_{L^2}=1$ and weak gradient zero. Local convolution shows that a function with zero weak gradient is constant on each connected coordinate ball; overlapping balls and connectedness make $w$ constant on $M^\circ$. Its trace is zero because $w\in H_0^1(M)$, while [F9] makes the trace of a nonzero constant equal that same nonzero boundary value. This contradiction proves the inequality.

Compactness of $M$ and positivity of $\gamma$ give $\gamma_*:=\min_M\gamma>0$. Thus $a_\gamma(w,z)=\int_M\gamma\,g(\nabla w,\nabla\bar z)\,dV_g$ is bounded on $H_0^1(M)$ and $a_\gamma(w,w)\geq c\|w\|_{H^1(M)}^2$ by step 1.1 and $\gamma_*$. By [F3], for any bounded conjugate-linear functional $G$ on $H_0^1(M)$ there is a unique $w\in H_0^1(M)$ with $a_\gamma(w,z)=G(z)$ for all $z$.

Flatten each boundary chart, apply the local half-space trace lift, and patch the finitely many chart lifts with a smooth partition. The resulting $Ef\in H^1(M)$ has trace $f$ and norm bounded by $C\|f\|_{H^{1/2}(\partial M)}$ by [F5]. For $h\in L^2(M)$ take $G(z)=-\int_Mh\overline z\,dV_g-a_\gamma(Ef,z)$ in step 2.1 and set $v=Ef+w$. Then $v$ has trace $f$ and satisfies the weak equation. If $v_1,v_2$ are two such solutions, their difference has zero global trace, hence lies in $H_0^1(M)$ by [F10]. Its energy is zero; since $\gamma\geq\gamma_*>0$, its gradient vanishes, and step 1.1 gives $v_1=v_2$.

Suppose $h$ and $f$ are smooth. By [F8], extend $f$ smoothly from the boundary into a collar and multiply by a cutoff to obtain a smooth extension $Ef$ on $M$. Then $w=v-Ef$ has zero trace, so $w\in H_0^1(M)$ by [F10], and solves $\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gw)=h-\operatorname{div}_g(\gamma\nabla_gEf)$, whose right-hand side is smooth. In each boundary chart, flatten the boundary and write the principal matrix as $|g|^{1/2}\gamma g^{ij}$; it is smooth and uniformly elliptic because $g$ is positive definite and $\gamma$ has a positive minimum. For the base case, localize $w$ by a cutoff; its equation has an $L^2$ right-hand side since $w\in H^1$, so [F6] gives local $H^2$ regularity. If $w\in H^{m+1}$, each cutoff commutator contains derivatives of $w$ of order at most $m+1$ with smooth bounded coefficients, hence lies in $H^m$; the localized right-hand side is therefore in $H^m$, and [F6] gives $H^{m+2}$ regularity. Induction over $m$ and a finite chart cover give $w\in H^m(M)$ for every integer $m$. By [F7], $w$ and hence $v=Ef+w$ are smooth up to the boundary.

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$ and let $p\in M$. Then there exist
$h>0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a smooth map

$$ \Phi:(-h,h)\times U\to M $$

such that for every $q\in U$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,q)$ is the unique
integral curve of $X$ on $(-h,h)$ with initial value $\Phi(0,q)=q$.

derivations.claim: Embed the segment in a collar extension across $\partial M_0$ and cover it by finitely many coordinate neighborhoods. On an embedded subsegment, parallel transport an orthonormal normal frame and set $F(t,y)=\exp_{\gamma(t)}(\sum_\alpha y_\alpha E_\alpha(t))$. The inverse function theorem gives local Fermi coordinates with $g_{jk}(t,0)=\delta_{jk}$ and $\partial_i g_{jk}(t,0)=0$. This construction is along an interval and uses no orientation of $M_0$.

In one such chart, seek $v_s=e^{is\Theta}a$, $s=\tau+i\lambda$, with $\Theta(t,0)=t$ and $\operatorname{Im}\Theta(t,y)\geq c|y|^2$. Expand $\Theta$ into homogeneous transverse Taylor polynomials. The quadratic polynomial is $\frac12H(t)y\cdot y$; substituting into $g(d\Theta,d\Theta)=1$ gives the matrix Riccati equation $H'+H^2=F(t)$, where $F$ is determined by the second transverse Taylor coefficient of the inverse metric. An initial complex symmetric $H(t_0)$ with positive-definite imaginary part yields a smooth solution with positive imaginary part on a short subsegment. Each higher homogeneous phase term then solves a linear first-order ODE along $t$, because its newest coefficient occurs linearly in the eikonal equation.

Write $m=\dim M_0$, so the transverse dimension is $m-1$. citations.quote: A transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$ is a compact connected smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian domain $(M,g)$ with smooth boundary, together with a compact connected smooth $(n-1)$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with boundary $(M_0,g_0)$ and an isometric embedding of $(M,g)$ as a smooth domain compactly contained in $(\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ,dx_1^2\oplus g_0)$. The coordinate $x_1$ on $\mathbb R$ is the distinguished Euclidean coordinate; $M_0$ is the transversal manifold. All Laplacians use $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g$. Neither $M$ nor $M_0$ is assumed orientable. A positive smooth conformal factor is not included in this definition; claims using a conformally related metric must state and prove the required conformal transformation separately.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, with no orientability assumption. Fix a finite smooth atlas of interior and boundary charts and a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it. For an integer $k\geq0$, define $H^k(M)$ as the completion of $C^\infty(M)$ in the sum of the Euclidean $W^{k,2}$ norms of the localized coordinate representatives; derivatives in a boundary chart are taken on the corresponding half-space. Define $H_0^1(M)$ as the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in $H^1(M)$. Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. Define $H^{-1/2}(\partial M)$ as the continuous dual of $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ with the Riemannian boundary density pairing. These are the fixed-atlas norms used on this page; no atlas-independence assertion is part of this definition.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. At each interior point, the
**Laplace–Beltrami operator** of $g$ is defined by the metric trace of the Hessian,
$$\Delta_gf(p):=\operatorname{tr}_g(\operatorname{Hess}f)_p:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i),$$
where $n=\dim M$ and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is any $g_p$-orthonormal basis of $T_pM$; the
trace of a bilinear form with respect to a positive-definite inner product does not
depend on that choice, so $\Delta_gf$ is well-defined and smooth in the interior;
when $f$ is smooth up to the boundary, it has the usual one-sided extension there.
Here
$\operatorname{Hess}f(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\operatorname{grad}f,Y)$ is the Levi-Civita
Hessian of
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]].

Equivalently, and with the **positive-divergence convention** of this library,
$$\Delta_gf=\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f),$$
where $\operatorname{div}_gX=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_vX)$ is the Riemannian
divergence of [[def-riemannian-divergence]] as computed in
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]]. The equivalence is the
pointwise computation
$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$
the middle sum being the endomorphism trace of $v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f$
in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with
$\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f)$; no local coordinates are needed and no
analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold
both sides are the empty sum $0$, and on a manifold with boundary the operator is defined
at interior points, with the usual one-sided extension at boundary points when $f$ is
smooth up to the boundary.

**This definition is the pointwise geometric operator only.** It records the trace
formula, the divergence form and the sign convention
$\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\circ\operatorname{grad}$ fixed by
[[def-riemannian-divergence]]. It does not assert any analytic conclusion about
harmonic functions on manifolds — no maximum principle, no Harnack inequality, no
boundary-value solvability, no spectral theory, and no Liouville theorem. Those are
separate results with their own hypotheses, and their Euclidean forms are not licensed
on a general Riemannian manifold merely by writing down this definition.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a complex normed space, let $M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, and
let $f_0:M \to \mathbb{C}$ be a bounded complex linear functional. Then there
exists a bounded complex linear functional $F:X \to \mathbb{C}$ such that
$F|_M=f_0$ and $\|F\|=\|f_0\|$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and let $f$ be a bounded linear functional on $H$ (The dual space X^* of a normed space and its dual norm). Then there is a unique $y\in H$ with

$$f(x)=\langle x,y\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in H,$$

and $\|f\|=\|y\|$, where $\|f\|$ is the dual norm (The operator norm as the least bound and as the unit-sphere or unit-ball supremum). Under the first-variable-linear convention the representing vector depends conjugate-linearly and isometrically on $f$: if $f_i$ is represented by $y_i$ and $a,b$ are scalars, then $af_1+bf_2$ is represented by $\overline a\,y_1+\overline b\,y_2$.

abla_g\psi|^2+2h
abla_g\psi\cdot
abla_g+h\Delta_g\psi.$$ For $\psi=s$, $|
abla s|=1$ and $\Delta s=0$, so $P_{s,h,0}=A+C$ with $A=-h^2\Delta_g-1$ self-adjoint and $C=2h\partial_s$ skew-adjoint on compactly supported functions.

Convexify by $\psi=f(s)=s+\frac{h}{2\varepsilon}s^2$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is fixed small and then $h/\varepsilon$ is small. Since $M$ is compact, choose $h$ so $f'=1+hs/\varepsilon>1/2$ on $M$. The conjugated operator is $P_{\psi,h,0}=A_\varepsilon+C_\varepsilon$ with $$A_\varepsilon=-h^2\Delta_g-(f')^2,\qquad C_\varepsilon=2hf'\partial_s+hf'',\qquad f''=h/\varepsilon.$$ Here $A_\varepsilon$ is self-adjoint and $C_\varepsilon$ is skew-adjoint. Product independence of $s$ makes $-\Delta_g=-\partial_s^2-\Delta_{g_0}$, with $\Delta_{g_0}$ commuting with $C_\varepsilon$. Direct differentiation in the $s$ coordinate therefore gives the exact commutator $$[A_\varepsilon,C_\varepsilon]=4h(f')^2f''-4h^3f''\partial_s^2.$$ For compactly supported $w$, integration by parts yields $$\|P_{\psi,h,0}w\|_2^2 =\|A_\varepsilon w\|_2^2+\|C_\varepsilon w\|_2^2+ 4h f''\|(f')w\|_2^2+4h^3f''\|\partial_sw\|_2^2 \geq c h^2\varepsilon^{-1}\|w\|_2^2.$$ The same identity implies $\|A_\varepsilon w\|_2\leq\|P_{\psi,h,0}w\|_2$. Since $\|h\nabla w\|_2^2=\langle A_\varepsilon w,w\rangle+\|f'w\|_2^2$, the $L^2$ bound just obtained gives $\|w\|_2+\|h\nabla w\|_2\leq C_\varepsilon h^{-1}\|P_{\psi,h,0}w\|_2$.

The convexified and unconvexified weights are related by multiplication with $m=e^{s^2/(2\varepsilon)}$: $P_{\psi,h,0}(mw)=mP_{s,h,0}w$. On compact $M$, $m$ and $m^{-1}$ are bounded, so step 2.1 yields $\|w\|_2\leq C h^{-1}\|P_{s,h,0}w\|_2$. Adding the potential changes the conjugated operator by $h^2q$. Its norm on $w$ is at most $h^2\|q\|_\infty\|w\|_2$, which is absorbed in the preceding estimate for sufficiently small $h$. Replacing $s$ by either sign of $x_1$ proves the a priori estimate in the statement.

Let $P=P_{\varphi,h,q}$ and apply the a priori estimate also to $P^*=P_{-\varphi,h,q}$, which has the same real potential and the opposite allowed sign. On $E=P^*(C_c^\infty(M^\circ))\subset L^2(M)$ define the complex-linear functional $\ell(P^*w)=\int_M\bar Fw\,dV_g$. The estimate makes this well-defined: $P^*w=0$ implies $w=0$. It also gives $|\ell(P^*w)|\leq\|F\|_2\|w\|_2\leq Ch^{-1}\|F\|_2\|P^*w\|_2$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume Countable Choice.

Define $H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ by the fixed finite boundary atlas and partition of unity, using the Euclidean fractional Slobodeckij space $W^{1/2,2}(\mathbb R^{n-1})$ for each localized representative. For complex scalars, define it as the continuous conjugate-linear dual: its pairing with $h\in H^{1/2}(\partial M)$ is linear in the dual element and conjugate-linear in $h$, using the Riemannian boundary density. then $(Tu)|_{\partial\Omega\cap\partial\Omega'}=T_{\Omega'}(u|_{\Omega'})$

bounded $C^1$ domain in the graph sense of

chart-independent surface measure of
[[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]] and

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

A transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$ is a compact connected smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian domain $(M,g)$ with smooth boundary, together with a compact connected smooth $(n-1)$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with boundary $(M_0,g_0)$ and an isometric embedding of $(M,g)$ as a smooth domain compactly contained in $(\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ,dx_1^2\oplus g_0)$. The coordinate $x_1$ on $\mathbb R$ is the distinguished Euclidean coordinate; $M_0$ is the transversal manifold. All Laplacians use $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla_g$. Neither $M$ nor $M_0$ is assumed orientable. A positive smooth conformal factor is not included in this definition; claims using a conformally related metric must state and prove the required conformal transformation separately.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a transversally anisotropic product domain, let $q\in C^\infty(\overline M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\varphi=\sigma x_1$ for $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}$. For $0<h\leq h_0$ define
$$P_{\varphi,h,q}=e^{\varphi/h}h^2(-\Delta_g+q)e^{-\varphi/h}.$$
There is a constant $C$ such that every $w\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ satisfies
$$\|w\|_{L^2(M)}\leq Ch^{-1}\|P_{\varphi,h,q}w\|_{L^2(M)}.$$
Moreover, for every $F\in L^2(M)$ there is an $R\in L^2(M)$ solving $P_{\varphi,h,q}R=F$ in distributions on $M^\circ$ and satisfying
$$\|R\|_{L^2(M)}\leq Ch^{-1}\|F\|_{L^2(M)}.$$
No boundary trace is prescribed for $R$.

For a smooth real function $f$, its **Riemannian gradient** is $\operatorname{grad}_g f=(df)^\sharp$.

[[prop-exterior-derivative-of-a-function-is-its-differential]] identifies $df(X)=Xf$. The smooth bundle isomorphism in [[thm-the-musical-maps-are-smooth-inverse-bundle-isomorphisms]] therefore makes the gradient a smooth vector field. In coordinates $(\operatorname{grad}_g f)^i=\sum_jg^{ij}\partial_jf$. Constants, and all functions in dimension zero, have zero gradient.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Riemannian manifold, possibly with boundary, and let
$f:M\to\mathbb R$ be smooth. At each interior point, the
**Laplace–Beltrami operator** of $g$ is defined by the metric trace of the Hessian,
$$\Delta_gf(p):=\operatorname{tr}_g(\operatorname{Hess}f)_p:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i),$$
where $n=\dim M$ and $e_1,\dots,e_n$ is any $g_p$-orthonormal basis of $T_pM$; the
trace of a bilinear form with respect to a positive-definite inner product does not
depend on that choice, so $\Delta_gf$ is well-defined and smooth in the interior;
when $f$ is smooth up to the boundary, it has the usual one-sided extension there.
Here
$\operatorname{Hess}f(X,Y)=g(\nabla_X\operatorname{grad}f,Y)$ is the Levi-Civita
Hessian of
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]].

Equivalently, and with the **positive-divergence convention** of this library,
$$\Delta_gf=\operatorname{div}_g(\operatorname{grad}f),$$
where $\operatorname{div}_gX=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_vX)$ is the Riemannian
divergence of [[def-riemannian-divergence]] as computed in
[[prop-gradient-hessian-and-divergence-connection-formulas]]. The equivalence is the
pointwise computation
$$\sum_i\operatorname{Hess}f(e_i,e_i)=\sum_i g(\nabla_{e_i}\operatorname{grad}f,e_i)=\operatorname{tr}(v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f),$$
the middle sum being the endomorphism trace of $v\mapsto\nabla_v\operatorname{grad}f$
in the orthonormal basis $(e_i)$, which the same supplier identifies with

analytic regularity beyond the smoothness of $f$ is used. On a zero-dimensional manifold

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact transversally anisotropic product domain of dimension $n\geq3$ and let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$. Fix an integer $s>n/2+2$ and a finite family $h_1,\ldots,h_m\in C^\infty(\partial M,\mathbb C)$. For $\epsilon=(\epsilon_1,\ldots,\epsilon_m)\in\mathbb R^m$ sufficiently near zero, the equation
$$-\Delta_g u+q u^3=0\quad\text{in }M^\circ,\qquad u|_{\partial M}=\sum_{j=1}^m\epsilon_jh_j$$
has a unique solution in a fixed small $H^s(M)$ ball. The parameter map $\epsilon\mapsto u_\epsilon$ is $C^3$ into $H^s(M)$, and the corresponding nonlinear Dirichlet-to-Neumann data $\partial_{\nu_{\rm out}}u_\epsilon|_{\partial M}$ is $C^3$ into $C^0(\partial M)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $(M,g)$ be a compact smooth Riemannian domain with smooth boundary, let $q\in C^\infty(M,\mathbb R)$, and let $\Lambda_q^{\rm NL}$ be the small-data nonlinear Dirichlet-to-Neumann map for $-\Delta_g u+qu^3=0$. For smooth boundary directions $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$, let $v_j$ be the harmonic solution with boundary value $h_j$. If
$$w_{123}=\left.\partial_{\epsilon_1}\partial_{\epsilon_2}\partial_{\epsilon_3}u_\epsilon\right|_{\epsilon=0},$$
where $u_\epsilon$ has boundary value $\epsilon_1h_1+\epsilon_2h_2+\epsilon_3h_3$, then
$$-\Delta_gw_{123}+6qv_1v_2v_3=0,\qquad w_{123}|_{\partial M}=0,$$
and
$$\left\langle (D^3\Lambda_q^{\rm NL})_0[h_1,h_2,h_3],h_4\right\rangle =6\int_Mq\,v_1v_2v_3\overline{v_4}\,dV_g.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice.

Let $M\Subset\mathbb R\times M_0^\circ$ be a three-dimensional transversally anisotropic product domain with compact connected simple surface transversal $(M_0,g_0)$. For every $p\in M_0^\circ$ choose two nontangential unit-speed geodesic segments $\gamma_1,\gamma_2$ meeting transversely at $p$ and nowhere else. For every $\xi\in\mathbb R$ and every $Q\in C^\infty(\overline M)$, there are four exact harmonic solutions $u_{\tau,1}^+,u_{\tau,1}^-,u_{\tau,2}^+,u_{\tau,2}^-\in H^1(M)$, with no prescribed boundary values, such that
$$\lim_{\tau\to\infty}\int_MQ(x_1,x')u_{\tau,1}^+u_{\tau,1}^-u_{\tau,2}^+u_{\tau,2}^-\,dV_g =c(p,\gamma_1,\gamma_2)\int_{I_p}e^{-i\xi x_1}Q(x_1,p)\,dx_1,$$
where $I_p=\{x_1\in\mathbb R:(x_1,p)\in M^\circ\}$ and $c(p,\gamma_1,\gamma_2)>0$ is the nonzero Gaussian normalization divided by $|\sin\angle(\dot\gamma_1(p),\dot\gamma_2(p))|$.
Assume countable choice. If $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb C)$ and $\widehat f=\widehat g$, then $f=g$ almost everywhere. Equality of the transforms almost everywhere already suffices.

derivations.claim: Fix four smooth boundary directions $h_1,h_2,h_3,h_4$. Equality of the finite-parameter DN maps for $q_1$ and $q_2$ implies equality of their mixed third derivatives at the origin. Applying [F2] to each coefficient and subtracting gives $$\int_M(q_1-q_2)v_1v_2v_3\overline{v_4}\,dV_g=0$$ for every four harmonic functions $v_j$ arising from smooth boundary data.

The identity in step 1.1 holds also for complex smooth harmonic functions: write their boundary values as real and imaginary parts and expand the separately linear or conjugate-linear expression. Since the Laplacian has real coefficients, conjugation preserves harmonicity; replacing the fourth function by its conjugate therefore gives $\int_M Qw_1w_2w_3w_4\,dV=0$ for every four smooth complex harmonic functions, where $Q=q_1-q_2$.

Fix $p\in M_0^\circ$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R$. Choose the transverse boundary-to-boundary geodesic segments through $p$ supplied by [F3] (their existence is established in that supplier's proof). Apply [F3] with $Q=q_1-q_2$. Its witnesses are smooth by [F5], so their product integral is zero for every $\tau$ by step 2.1. Taking their stated limit gives $$c(p,\gamma_1,\gamma_2)\int_{I_p}e^{-i\xi x_1}(q_1-q_2)(x_1,p)\,dx_1=0,$$ where $c>0$ is the crossing normalization. The coefficient transform therefore vanishes for every $\xi$ and every $p$.

For each $p$, extend $x_1\mapsto(q_1-q_2)(x_1,p)$ by zero outside $I_p$. It is a compactly supported $L^1(\mathbb R)$ function. By step 3.1, [F4] makes this section zero almost everywhere; its smoothness in the interior of $M$ then makes $q_1-q_2=0$ on $M^\circ$, and continuity gives equality on $\overline M$. Thus the theorem follows.

Indeed the conjugated residual is $(-\Delta_{g_0}-s^2)v_s+q_jv_s$, of bounded $L^2$ norm on a fixed product cylinder; multiplication by $e^{\pm i\lambda x_1}$ is bounded there. Correcting with the real-weight solver gives precisely this bound. Their product in step 1.1 is $e^{-2i\lambda x_1}(v_s+r_1)(\overline{v_s}+\overline{r_2})$. Every error integral tends to zero by Cauchy--Schwarz, the boundedness of $Q$, $\|v_s\|_2=O(1)$, and $\|r_j\|_2=o(1)$. Integrating first in $x_1$ gives the smooth compactly supported transversal test function $\widehat Q_\lambda$ below. Step 2.1 supplies $$\int_{\gamma}\widehat Q_\lambda(\gamma(t))e^{-2\lambda t}\,dt=0 \quad\text{for every real }\lambda\text{ and every nontangential geodesic }\gamma,$$ where $\widehat Q_\lambda(x')=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-2i\lambda x_1}Q(x_1,x')\,dx_1$.
